source: Liu et al. (2026) What Do LLM Agents Know About Their World? Task2Quiz
finding: Closest thing found to a quiz-after-experience probe for agents (GAP 1, 8). After an agent explores a text game, a deterministic quiz measures what it knows about the world. Task success is a poor proxy for that knowledge. Memory systems (Mem0, LangMem, A-Mem) did not reliably beat simply keeping the full context.
numbers: 30 environments, 224 tasks, 1,967 grounded QA pairs. Example rows: in-context 52.41 vs Mem0 52.36 vs LangMem 54.55 total quiz score for one model; for other models in-context sits at or above memory systems. Weakest on property and latent-state questions.
quote: task success is often a poor proxy for environment understanding
limits: The quiz is used only as a measurement, not as practice. Nothing is fed back to the agent. Table text is garbled by PDF extraction, so only the pattern is reliable.
agent_relevance: Gives a gap-detection metric (quiz on world state) that could be reused to test whether self-quizzing exposes holes. It is not itself a testing-effect test.

source: Yuan, Su, Yao (2026) Diagnosing Retrieval vs. Utilization Bottlenecks in LLM Agent Memory
finding: 3x3 study of write strategy by retrieval method on LoCoMo. Retrieval method dominates. Raw chunks with zero LLM calls match or beat costly extraction or summary. Failures mostly happen at retrieval, not at use.
numbers: Accuracy spans 20 points across retrieval methods vs 3 to 8 points across write strategies. Basic RAG 77.9% (cosine), 81.1% (hybrid). Hybrid averages 77.2%, cosine 73.4%, BM25 57.1%. Hybrid cuts retrieval failures roughly in half (35.3% to 11.4% for Basic RAG).
limits: One benchmark (LoCoMo), judged by an LLM (92% agreement with humans on the validation sample). No self-testing arm.
agent_relevance: Retrieval, not rehearsal, is the lever in current agent memory. Supports not adding a self-quiz operator just to improve storage.

source: ARISE (2026) Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
finding: Agent attributes its own failures, stores corrections, consolidates them into rules, and accepts a rule only if held-out accuracy rises. This is an error-then-feedback loop, the nearest agent analogue to test-with-feedback (GAP 1, 5).
numbers: 14 domains from SOP-Bench and tau2-bench, 5 models. ARISE-Teacher +10.9 points SOP-Bench, +5.8 tau2-bench. ARISE-Self (model diagnoses itself) +10.0 SOP-Bench. 4.0% fewer calls, 5.2% fewer output tokens, per-task cost -1.0%.
limits: Abstract only. Gains come from learning from failures on tasks, not from quizzing on studied text. Teacher and self variants are different arms; no re-reading control.
agent_relevance: Self-diagnosis alone gets almost all of the teacher gain (10.0 vs 10.9), which fits the idea that checking against a verifier is what helps. Held-out acceptance gate matches our guardrail style.

source: Audit of a self-learning migration agent (2026) Does a Self-Learning Migration Agent Learn?
finding: Apparent gains from experience memory in an agent were mostly leakage. Once leak-free units are used the memory effect vanishes. Warns that any agent self-practice study needs a leak check (GAP 1).
numbers: 1,833 pairs; 72% (264 of 367) held-out units shared a reference with training. Memory effect 0.015 [0.004, 0.025] fell to 0.002 [-0.008, 0.011] on 103 leak-free units. Copy baseline RC 0.222 beat every LLM system (max 0.163). Retrieval margin fell 54% as the knowledge base grew from 12 to 1,200 entries.
limits: Abstract only. One task domain (Oracle to PostgreSQL).
agent_relevance: A direct warning: if we ever test agent self-quizzing, repeated or overlapping items will fake a testing effect.

source: An, Liu, Acharya, Hashmi (2025) Enhancing Student Learning with LLM-Generated Retrieval Practice Questions
finding: Closes part of GAP 7 negatively: still no large randomised comparison. The study is quasi-experimental, about 60 students, two courses. Weeks with LLM multiple-choice practice were compared with weeks without any practice, not with instructor quizzes.
numbers: Mean quiz accuracy 89% with LLM practice vs 73% without. 10-week quarter, weeks 6-9, two 2-week cycles (practice week then quiz week). Same students in both cycles, quizzes anonymous, treated as independent groups.
limits: Not randomised. Cycle order fixed (practice first, control second), so time and quiz difficulty are confounded. No instructor-quiz arm. Quizzes differ between cycles.
agent_relevance: Only shows that some practice beats none. Not evidence that LLM quizzes equal instructor quizzes.

source: An and Wang (2026) Student Use of LLMs and the Limits of AI-Generated Question Difficulty in Data Science Courses
finding: LLM-assigned difficulty on retrieval practice questions does not predict real difficulty. This undermines using an LLM to tune desirable difficulty (GAP 4, 7).
numbers: 378 authored questions, 311 deployed, 7,888 student responses. Difficulty label vs Bloom level Spearman 0.90 (co-generation artifact). Difficulty label vs empirical difficulty 0.06; Bloom level 0.02.
limits: Single institution, data science courses. Measures item difficulty, not learning gain.
agent_relevance: An agent cannot trust its own predicted difficulty for choosing what to self-test; measure success rate directly.

source: Boustani and Shanks (2022) Heterogeneity and Publication Bias in Research on Test-Potentiated New Learning
finding: Re-analysis of Chan et al. (2018) shows large publication bias. The forward (test-potentiated new learning) effect shrinks to nothing under bias correction. Standard-design effects survive 3PSM but not PET.
numbers: Chan et al. overall g=0.44 [0.35,0.53] (k=159, Q=1133.94). After 3PSM g=0.02 [-0.14,0.18]; after PET g=-0.02 [-0.26,0.22]. Standard designs 0.75 -> 0.52 (3PSM) -> -0.08 (PET). Pre-test designs 0.34 (k=45, little bias). Interleaved -0.56. Published studies g=0.50 vs unpublished 0.19.
limits: About forward testing, not the plain test-vs-restudy effect. PET is known to over-correct with heavy heterogeneity (I2 about 88%).
agent_relevance: Closes GAP 3 in spirit: publication-bias correction can remove a large share of a testing-effect meta-analytic mean. Treat g=0.50 style figures as upper bounds.

source: Pan and Rickard (2018) Transfer of test-enhanced learning: meta-analytic review
finding: Opened in full. Moderators survive bias correction but intercepts shrink. The no-moderator transfer intercept is about zero after PEESE.
numbers: 192 effect sizes, 122 experiments, 67 papers, N=10,396; d=0.40 [0.31,0.50]. No response congruency: d=0.28. PEESE: response congruency adds 0.36, elaborated retrieval adds 0.18, intercept 0 (d=0.015). Selection-model intercept 0.12 under moderate one-tailed bias, negative under severe.
limits: Transfer to different tests, not direct retention. N in abstract is 10,396 (earlier note said 10,382).
agent_relevance: Good for GAP 10: effects stack and depend on match between practice and test.

source: Pan and Rickard (2018) Transfer meta-analysis: initial test performance and three-factor framework
finding: Answers GAP 4 and 10 together. Initial retrieval success, response congruency and elaborated retrieval jointly predict transfer. The best recipe is not any single moderator.
numbers: Subset with initial-test data: moderators significant at p<=.015. Low initial success, no congruency, no elaboration: d about -0.05 [-0.22,0.12]. All three at best level (initial accuracy 0.98): predicted d=0.90 [0.71,1.08] (random effects) and 0.58 (PEESE). PEESE moderator values: congruency 0.25, initial accuracy 0.50.
limits: Predictions extrapolate to edges of the data (lowest initial proportion correct 0.19, highest 0.98). Initial-test data were available only for part of the dataset.
agent_relevance: For LLM self-checks: success rate is measurable, so one can bin by it. Effects from a 75% threshold are better described as a slope than a cut-off.

source: Karpicke (2025) Retrieval-based learning chapter: bifurcation account and forgetting rate
finding: Bifurcation (Kornell, Bjork, Garcia 2011): recalled items get a large boost, unrecalled items get none, restudy gives every item a small boost, forgetting rate equal. This explains the crossover. Karpicke calls the benefit in that account an item-selection artifact and cites two lines of evidence that retrieval does change forgetting rate.
numbers: Verbal model. No fitted numbers in the chapter.
limits: Read via the chapter, original Kornell et al. paper not opened (GAP 9 only partly closed). The two lines of evidence were not followed up.
agent_relevance: Maps to agents: an item that fails to be retrieved and gets no feedback is simply not repaired. Feedback is the repair path for failures.

source: Karpicke (2025) chapter: short answer vs multiple choice and feedback (Kang 2007, Little 2012, Butler and Roediger 2007, McDaniel 2007)
finding: Answers GAP 5 and 4 together. Feedback and initial success decide whether short answer beats multiple choice. Without feedback MC wins because it is easier; with feedback short answer wins slightly. Butler and Roediger found no effect of feedback on items at one month.
numbers: Kang 2007 Exp 1: initial MC 86% vs short answer 54% correct. Butler and Roediger: 68% short answer vs 88% MC initial success; at 1 month short answer best, MC no better than rereading. Little 2012: no feedback MC > SA; with feedback SA slightly > MC.
limits: Secondary description by Karpicke, no new effect sizes. Evidence on feedback is mixed between studies.
agent_relevance: Feedback against a source is the active ingredient in repair. Check-against-source steps in our scaffold are justified by this, but the Rowland delayed-feedback cell is small.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) Instruction-tuned Language Models are Better Knowledge Learners: ablations on order
finding: Re-read ablations for GAP 6. Question exposure helps most when it comes before the documents. The paper does not test newer models, but the order effect is clear in Llama-2 7B.
numbers: EM (Llama-2 7B): QA before doc grouped 38.2 vs QA after doc grouped 27.2; interleaved 45.9 vs 43.2. Train QA then train QA plus doc, then test doc: 48.1. After document training, accuracy on the train questions fell from almost perfect to 30%. Plain continued pretraining 27.2 (text) vs 27.6 (table).
limits: Only Llama-2 7B/70B on 2023 Wikipedia text. No replication on newer models found in this search. Format matching and retrieval practice cannot be separated in these ablations.
agent_relevance: Closer to format matching (transfer-appropriate processing) than to retrieval practice. Not evidence for a testing effect in agents.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Self-Tuning: Instructing LLMs to Acquire New Knowledge through Self-Teaching
finding: Extension of PIT using self-generated memorization, comprehension and self-reflection tasks (inspired by the Feynman technique). Tested on three base models, not only Llama-2.
numbers: Llama2-7B, Qwen2-7B, Mistral-7B-v0.1 reported; three Wiki-Newpages-2023 sets (Bio, Multi, Film); results averaged over three runs, p<0.001. About 13% commonsense accuracy gain and about 1% F1 on retained knowledge vs closed-book baseline.
limits: Partly opened (abstract, setup, retention paragraph). Not a testing-effect test: tasks are training data augmentation. Models are still 2023-2024 era open models.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to GAP 6: the pattern repeats across 3 base models, but no 2025-2026 frontier model test was found.

source: Cao, Schooler, Zafarani (2025) Analyzing Memory Effects in LLMs through the Lens of Cognitive Psychology
finding: Seven human memory effects tested in LLMs. The testing effect is not among them. Shows list length, list strength, fan, false memory and cross-domain transfer; no U-shaped serial position at tested lengths.
numbers: Seven phenomena listed in the abstract: list length, list strength, fan effect, false memory, cross-domain generalization, serial position, meaningful vs nonsense material. Fan effect: hit rate near ceiling, false alarms up.
limits: A text search of the full paper found no testing effect or retrieval practice test. In-context memory, not weights.
agent_relevance: Closes GAP 1 negatively for this paper: nobody has run Roediger-style test vs restudy inside an LLM context here.

source: OSF preprint (2025) Research on the Testing Effect Routinely Conflates Direct and Forward Testing Effects: meta-analysis with free recall
finding: Only about a third of free-recall testing effects isolate the direct effect. Mixed studies give larger effects. The literature is a mixture.
numbers: 67% of testing effects from mixed studies, 33% from direct studies; mixed larger than direct.
limits: Preprint, abstract via OSF API only. Not peer reviewed in this source.
agent_relevance: Supports caution on pooled numbers like g=0.50. Pairs with d07.

source: OSF preprint (2025) The testing effect occurs with both coherent and incoherent text (replication of de Jonge et al. 2015)
finding: Higher-powered replication and extension. The testing effect did not depend on text complexity or on test type. Counts against one claimed boundary condition (GAP 2, partly).
numbers: Experiment 1 N=111 (fill-in-the-blank, 1-week delay); Experiment 2 N=117 (short-answer practice). Testing effect present for both coherent and scrambled text.
limits: Abstract only. Two small experiments, not multi-site, not a replication of Roediger and Karpicke 2006.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a claimed boundary condition does not hold; effect is robust to material structure.

source: OSF preprint (2026) Event memory is strengthened and integrated by review: retrieval practice offers inconsistent additional benefit
finding: Three pre-registered experiments found the classic testing effect weak to absent for person-object-location events. Review of either kind beat no review.
numbers: N=122 across 3 experiments. Retrieval beat restudy on subjective memory only; no reliable objective advantage. Associative inference advantage over restudy seen in Exp 1, not Exp 2-3.
limits: Abstract only. Naturalistic event material; sleep delay. Not a test of prose.
agent_relevance: One pre-registered null for materials unlike word lists or prose. Narrows the scope of the effect.

source: OSF preprint (2026) Retrieval practice in higher education: causality and content transfer in a gateway math course
finding: Large field study with randomised problem sets in three cohorts. Gains are real but small. Final exam gain shown only in one cohort.
numbers: n=636, 584, 571 students. Quiz gain 4 to 5 percentage points (LATE). Strongest on isomorphic items, limited on far transfer. Final exam LATE 8 points in one cohort, smaller nonsignificant in others.
limits: Abstract only. Instrumental-variable estimates, practice problems not memory tests.
agent_relevance: Large-N classroom evidence is smaller than lab effects; matches the g=0.50 vs d=4.03 gap noted in the critique.

source: OSF preprint (2026) What gets retrieved? Testing effects in the absence of prior study
finding: Answering questions about never-studied material, with feedback, matched full instruction that included a study passage. Supports feedback as the main active ingredient (GAP 5).
numbers: Two experiments (prequestions and postquestions). Practice-with-feedback-only equalled accuracy of conditions with a study passage; study trial added time, not learning.
limits: Abstract only; sample sizes not seen. Single research group, preprint.
agent_relevance: Matches the idea that checking against a source does the work. For an agent, a verifier-checked answer may be worth more than a re-read.

source: OSF preprint (2025) Learning from mistakes: objective and subjective error magnitudes predict the testing effect
finding: Error-driven learning account of the testing effect. Larger errors at practice predict more memory gain; perceived and predicted errors add effects.
numbers: Two color-wheel experiments; computational model WRAP-E.
limits: Abstract only; continuous-error task, not prose.
agent_relevance: A mechanism that predicts the value of surprise or error signals. Could inform how an agent weights failed self-checks.

source: Grimaldi and Karpicke (2012) When and why do retrieval attempts enhance subsequent encoding?
finding: Failed retrieval before study helps only when cue and target are related, and only with immediate study. A constrained retrieval attempt hurt.
numbers: Exp 1: .73 vs .56 related pairs (pretest vs none); unrelated no gain. Exp 2: .68 vs .57 (d=0.58), constrained pretest .39 vs .57. Exp 3: delayed study erased the effect.
limits: Word pairs only, small samples.
agent_relevance: Explains when an agent's wrong guess before a lookup would help: only if the guess is in the right semantic neighbourhood.

source: Rowland (2014) and Adesope et al. (2017) full texts: access attempt
finding: Could not open either full paper this session (hosts unreachable or blocked). Search snippets only confirm Adesope's conclusion that practice tests beat restudy and all other conditions, and that a secondary source gives g=0.70 for Adesope.
numbers: No new numbers. Rowland g=0.50 and Adesope g=0.70 remain unverified.
limits: GAP 3 stays open for publication-bias-corrected Rowland and Adesope estimates. Only Boustani and Shanks 2022 (d07) and Pan and Rickard 2018 (d08) give bias-corrected numbers, for related meta-analyses.
agent_relevance: None beyond earlier lines.
